title: What it will take for Canada to regain its measles elimination status
summary: The U.S., Bolivia and Mexico lost their measles elimination status this week, as Canada did this time last year. What would it take for Canada to regain its status?

image.caption: Signs in English and Low German warn of a measles alert at the Taber Community Health Clinic in Taber, Alta., on July 28, 2025. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Health·New
The U.S., Bolivia and Mexico lost their measles elimination status this week, as Canada did this time last year. What would it take for Canada to regain its status?
Experts say re-eliminating the preventable, sometimes deadly disease is important — and well within reach
The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles elimination status this week, following in Canada's footsteps.
Last November, Canada lost its measles elimination status after 27 years, during a two-year outbreak that infected more than 6,400 people. The outbreak was declared over on Oct. 19.

blocks.text: Regaining Canada's measles elimination status is well within reach, experts say — and crucial, given the health risks from the highly contagious, sometimes deadly and completely preventable disease.

In addition to fever and rash, about one in three people with measles will have one or more complications, including diarrhea, ear infections that can lead to permanent hearing loss, pneumonia, inflammation of the brain or seizures.

In the Canadian outbreak, two infants died — one in Alberta and one in Ontario — when they contracted measles in the womb and were born prematurely. Ten people have died in the U.S. so far this year, The Associated Press reports.
The U.S. has officially lost its measles elimination status

Jennifer Nuzzo, a professor of epidemiology and director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health in Rhode Island, told CBC News Tuesday that other countries that have regained their status show a path forward for the U.S. and Canada.

Venezuela and Brazil, for instance, "got vaccine rates up, they engaged with communities, they improved their surveillance, and they were able to regain their measles elimination status," Nuzzo said. "So it shows us that it's possible to turn things around."
Here's what it would take to restore Canada's measles elimination designation:
12 consecutive outbreak-free months

There are multiple criteria for earning measles elimination status. At its most basic level, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) requires one year without residents spreading the disease to declare a country measles-free. Canada lost its elimination status last year because its outbreak continued for more than 12 months.

blocks.text: Elimination doesn't require zero measles cases, but rather no outbreaks with continuous transmission from the same strain of the virus.
In a statement Tuesday, PAHO noted that Canada "has interrupted the chain of transmission" and is working to regain elimination status.
An action plan

PAHO, which is the regional arm of the World Health Organization, says countries must submit a corrective action plan outlining the strategies and measures they will implement, and then prove they have stopped the transmission of the outbreak strain for at least 12 months.
When Canada lost its status, PAHO said the country would present an action plan "focused on boosting immunization coverage, reinforcing surveillance systems, and ensuring rapid outbreak response."
The Public Health Agency of Canada's 2025-26 departmental results report also details in broad strokes a "Measles Action Plan for Canada".

Trudy Dyck, a community health representative at Alberta Health Services, takes part in a course related to the measles outbreak, at the Taber Health Centre in Taber, Alta., in October 2025. (Ahmed Zakot/Reuters)
95 per cent vaccine coverage

To achieve no ongoing outbreaks for 12 months, countries need a vaccination rate of about 95 per cent, experts say. At that rate, communities achieve herd immunity, which can protect those unable to be vaccinated, such as infants.

In recent years, Canada has been well below 95 per cent. A 2025 study estimated 92 per cent coverage with one dose, but found only 79 per cent received the recommended two doses of the highly effective measles-mumps-rubella vaccine.

"No matter who's in power in Canada or the U.S., what administration, political left, right, it doesn't matter, because what is important is the vaccination rates among the population," said Dr. Alon Vaisman, an infection control physician at Toronto's University Health Network.
Education of skeptical communities
Vaisman said the vaccination numbers he sees show transmission is likely occurring in pockets where there are low vaccination rates, rather than evenly across the whole population.

The Canadian outbreak, which began at a gathering in New Brunswick, was concentrated in some provinces within close-knit religious and culturally distinct communities, including Mennonite populations in Alberta and Ontario.

blocks.text: "So the work required to get back to elimination means investing and educating pockets of the population in Canada, U.S., to increase their vaccination rates," Vaisman said. He added that education should be non-judgmental and speak plainly about side effects.
"Luckily, the vaccine has very few, and basically no long-lasting, side effects," he said.

Dr. Lynora Saxinger, an infectious diseases specialist at the University of Alberta, said when Canada lost its status last year that countering organized disinformation about vaccine safety would require a formal, organized resistance. That includes making debunking videos and looking closely at how algorithms shape disinformation.

Nuzzo told CBC News that proper outreach takes a "ground game" — being out in communities and engaging with trusted leaders to explain why the vaccine is important and how severe the disease is.
Increased surveillance
Close surveillance is critical for measles elimination, PAHO says.

There have long been calls for Canada to improve surveillance of infectious diseases — especially given cuts to U.S. health institutions that could result in increased transmission across the border. Experts have called for timely collaboration across provincial and territorial boundaries.

After the loss of status, PHAC said online it is working with provinces, territories and other vaccination partners to enhance monitoring activities, and that it is "improving the quality of Canada's measles surveillance system."
CBC News has reached out to the Public Health Agency of Canada for more specifics about the surveillance improvements and other steps Canada has taken to regain elimination status.
With files from Tashauna Reid, Amina Zafar, Alexandra Mae Jones, The Canadian Press, The Associated Press and Reuters
